patient.name: Gary Holloman
patient.chiefComplaint: Unresponsive, found slumped at his desk

history.hpi: Coworker noticed the patient did not respond to a page for a 2:00 PM meeting. When she checked on him roughly ten minutes later, she found him slumped forward in his desk chair, not responding to her voice, but breathing on his own with loud snoring respirations. No known witnessed collapse, no reported seizure activity, no vomiting noted by the coworker.
history.lastOralIntake: Coworkers report he skipped lunch; his breakfast bar on the desk is only half-eaten. Exact time of last intake unknown.
history.events: Found unresponsive at his desk during a weekday afternoon; coworker called 911 immediately and stayed with him until EMS arrival.

scene.dispatch: Unknown medical, 47-year-old male unresponsive, coworkers on scene, office building third floor.
scene.location: Open-plan office, third floor of a downtown office building. Patient is slumped forward in a rolling desk chair at his workstation.
scene.safety: No hazards reported. Standard office environment, elevator access, coworkers present and cooperative, no signs of violence or struggle.
scene.bystanders: Coworker (Denise) found him unresponsive after he missed a scheduled 2:00 PM meeting; she reports he 'seemed fine this morning' but has limited additional history. No family present on scene.
visualCues: Patient slumped forward over the desk, head resting near keyboard
Half-eaten breakfast bar on desk; lunch untouched in a bag nearby
Weekly pill organizer visible in open desk drawer
No vomitus, blood, or obvious trauma visible
Office chair on wheels, patient not restrained by seatbelt or fall-prevention

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: Crew arrives to find a 47-year-old male slumped forward in his desk chair. He does not respond to his name or verbal commands but is breathing with loud, snoring respirations. A coworker is present with limited history.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Partially compromised by tongue/positional obstruction; loud snoring respirations while slumped forward
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Shallow, adequate rate, no visible accessory muscle use
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulse present, strong and rapid; skin pale and diaphoretic
clinicalPresentation.pupils: Equal, round, sluggishly reactive to light
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Withdraws from painful stimuli in all four extremities; no purposeful movement to voice
otherFindings: Slumped forward over desk in rolling chair
No visible trauma, no medical alert jewelry
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: Moans to sternal rub; no words

expectedActions.shortAction: Assess airway patency; reposition patient to open airway
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Airway: Make sure airway remains patent; reposition patient as needed
expectedActions.rationale: Snoring respirations while slumped forward indicate positional/tongue airway obstruction that must be corrected before further assessment.

expectedActions.shortAction: Assess breathing for respiratory depression; check SpO2
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Breathing: Look for respiratory depression; check SPO2, EtCO2, and CO detector readings
expectedActions.rationale: SpO2 of 91% on room air must be identified early to guide oxygen therapy.

expectedActions.shortAction: Determine AVPU and Glasgow Coma Score
expectedActions.rationale: Establishes baseline mental status for reassessment and documentation.
Hypoglycemia is a rapidly treatable and common cause of altered mental status; must be ruled in/out early per the AEIOU-TIPS differential.

transitions.condition: Within the first two minutes on scene, the crew reassesses airway patency, checks breathing and SpO2, determines AVPU/GCS, and obtains a blood glucose reading, which returns at 38 mg/dL.

The crew becomes preoccupied with bystander history-taking or scene logistics and delays airway reassessment, repositioning, and glucose check for more than three minutes; the patient's positional airway obstruction worsens.

phases.name: Primary survey completed
phases.description: The crew has completed a rapid primary survey and confirmed a blood glucose of 38 mg/dL. The patient remains unresponsive to voice, breathing but unable to protect his own airway, so oral glucose cannot be safely given.
phases.triggerCondition: Primary survey completed within the first two minutes; blood glucose returns critically low at 38 mg/dL, but the patient's depressed mental status and inability to protect his airway rule out oral glucose administration at the BLS level.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent after repositioning; snoring resolved with head positioning
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Shallow, adequate rate, no accessory muscle use
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulse present, strong and rapid; skin pale and diaphoretic
clinicalPresentation.pupils: Equal, round, sluggishly reactive to light
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Withdraws from painful stimuli in all four extremities
otherFindings: No signs of trauma on exposed skin
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: Moans to sternal rub; no words

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize oral glucose contraindicated; patient cannot protect his airway
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Conscious patient with a patent airway: Glucose, oral (in form of glucose tablets, glucose gel, tube of cake icing, etc.) Unconscious patient, or patients who are unable to protect their own airway: Dextrose IV – administer in incremental doses until mental status improves or maximum field dosing is reached
expectedActions.rationale: Oral glucose in a patient who cannot protect his airway risks aspiration; definitive dextrose/glucagon administration is outside BLS scope, making rapid transport the priority.

expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Administer oxygen if needed for air hunger or respiratory distress and titrate to a target SPO2 of 94–98%
expectedActions.rationale: SpO2 of 92% on room air warrants supplemental oxygen titrated to target range.

expectedActions.shortAction: Position patient laterally to protect airway and limit aspiration risk
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Patient positioning can significantly impact respiratory mechanics. Elevating the head or padding (shoulders, occiput) can assist with opening airway and respiratory mechanics. This can both improve the ability to ventilate and limit aspiration
expectedActions.rationale: An unresponsive patient with intact but depressed airway reflexes should be positioned to minimize aspiration risk during transport.

expectedActions.shortAction: Transport to closest appropriate receiving facility
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If hypoglycemia with continued symptoms, transport to closest appropriate receiving facility
expectedActions.rationale: Symptomatic hypoglycemia with depressed mental status that cannot be corrected at the BLS level requires prompt transport for definitive treatment.

expectedActions.shortAction: Reassess vital signs and mental status
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Reassess vital signs (pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, neurologic status assessment) and mental status
expectedActions.rationale: Ongoing reassessment detects deterioration or improvement and guides communication with the receiving facility.

transitions.condition: Crew applies oxygen titrated toward 94–98% SpO2, positions the patient laterally to protect the airway, and initiates rapid transport with an ALS intercept requested for definitive dextrose administration.
Crew fails to position the patient laterally or apply oxygen before moving to transport; the unprotected airway allows secretions/emesis to compromise breathing.

phases.name: Rapid transport initiated
phases.description: The patient is packaged, positioned laterally, receiving supplemental oxygen, and en route to the closest appropriate receiving facility with an ALS intercept requested for dextrose administration. Vital signs and mental status are reassessed en route.
phases.triggerCondition: Oxygen applied and lateral positioning completed; crew recognizes definitive treatment for symptomatic hypoglycemia in an unresponsive patient is beyond BLS scope and prioritizes rapid transport with ALS intercept.

clinicalPresentation.breathing: Improved rate and quality on supplemental oxygen
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulse present, strong; skin remains pale and diaphoretic
otherFindings: Lateral recovery position maintained on cot
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: Moans to sternal rub; no words

phases.name: Airway compromised
phases.description: Assessment and airway repositioning were delayed. The patient's positional airway obstruction has progressed: breathing is now irregular with audible gurgling, and oxygenation is dropping.
phases.triggerCondition: The crew delayed reassessing the airway, repositioning the patient, and/or applying oxygen for more than three minutes (or moved to transport without protecting the airway); secretions have pooled in the posterior pharynx and the patient's SpO2 has fallen.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Compromised; audible gurgling, secretions pooling in posterior pharynx
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Irregular, shallow, increased work of breathing
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulse present but weaker; skin cool, pale, mottled
clinicalPresentation.pupils: Equal, round, sluggishly reactive to light
otherFindings: No purposeful response to voice or painful stimuli beyond posturing

expectedActions.shortAction: Suction airway immediately to clear pooled secretions
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Suction airway: for significantly contaminated airways, consider utilizing a suction assisted laryngeal airway decontamination (SALAD) technique
expectedActions.rationale: Delayed airway management has allowed secretions to compromise oxygenation; suctioning is required before effective ventilation or positioning can help.

expectedActions.shortAction: Open airway with head tilt/chin lift and reposition immediately
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Open and maintain patent airway. If needed, Provide head tilt/chin lift, or jaw thrust if concern for potential spinal injury
expectedActions.rationale: Reestablishing a patent airway is the immediate priority given the falling SpO2 and gurgling respirations.
